clinicalPearls: Follicular bronchiolitis is a reactive hyperplasia of bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT), with lymphoid follicles bearing germinal centres distributed along bronchovascular bundles and compressing small airways.
It sits within the spectrum of pulmonary lymphoid hyperplasia and overlaps clinically and histologically with lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP).
Typical presentation is progressive breathlessness and cough, with recurrent infections when an underlying immunodeficiency is present.
Recognised associations include rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, common variable immunodeficiency and paediatric HIV infection; an idiopathic form also exists.
High-resolution CT characteristically shows centrilobular and peribronchial nodules with ground-glass opacity, and mosaic attenuation may be seen.
Lung function may be obstructive, restrictive or mixed, often with reduced gas transfer.
Histology shows polyclonal reactive follicles along the airways; immunohistochemistry and B-cell clonality studies are needed to exclude a marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma.
Treatment is directed at the underlying disorder, for example immunoglobulin replacement in common variable immunodeficiency or immunosuppression in connective tissue disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Follicular bronchiolitis results from polyclonal hyperplasia of bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT), the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue of the airways. Reactive lymphoid follicles with well-formed germinal centres accumulate along bronchovascular bundles and immediately adjacent to bronchiolar walls, causing extrinsic narrowing of the small airways and the resulting cough and airflow limitation. It represents antigen-driven or dysregulated lymphoid proliferation and forms part of a continuum of pulmonary lymphoid hyperplasia that includes lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia. The proliferation is characteristically polyclonal and reactive rather than clonal, which distinguishes it from pulmonary marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma. It arises in the setting of autoimmune connective tissue disease (notably rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren syndrome), humoral immunodeficiency such as common variable immunodeficiency, HIV infection (particularly in children), hypersensitivity and chronic infection, and may also be idiopathic.
additionalDifferentials: Low-grade marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma of the lung
Respiratory (cellular) bronchiolitis and other small-airway diseases
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest (centrilobular and peribronchial nodules, ground-glass opacity, mosaic attenuation)
Connective tissue disease serology (rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, ANA, anti-Ro and anti-La)
Immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte subsets to screen for common variable immunodeficiency, plus an HIV test
Pulmonary function tests including gas transfer
Surgical or transbronchial lung biopsy with immunohistochemistry
B-cell clonality studies to exclude lymphoma
Bronchoalveolar lavage to characterise lymphocytosis and exclude infection
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging or dominant nodule or mass, or systemic B-symptoms, suggesting an underlying or transformed lymphoma
Recurrent severe infections pointing to an underlying immunodeficiency
Demonstration of a monoclonal B-cell population on clonality testing
reference.prognosis: The course is often stable or slowly progressive, especially when the underlying condition is treated; the outlook is worse with progressive interstitial fibrosis or if an occult lymphoproliferative disorder is present.
pitfalls: Mistaking reactive follicular bronchiolitis for MALT lymphoma, or vice versa, without clonality studies.
Overlooking an underlying immunodeficiency such as common variable immunodeficiency or an associated connective tissue disease.
Relying on small transbronchial biopsies, which may be non-diagnostic given the airway-centred distribution.
Attributing centrilobular nodules solely to infection or hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
ATS/ERS classification of the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias
management: Treat the underlying associated disorder — immunoglobulin replacement for common variable immunodeficiency, antiretroviral therapy in HIV, and disease control of rheumatoid arthritis or Sjögren syndrome
Suppress the lymphoid proliferation with corticosteroids, adding a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant or an immunomodulatory macrolide in progressive or symptomatic disease
Provide symptomatic airway therapy with bronchodilators for airflow obstruction and pulmonary rehabilitation
Give infection prophylaxis and prompt antimicrobial treatment where an underlying immunodeficiency predisposes to recurrent infection
Monitor with serial pulmonary function tests and high-resolution CT for progression to interstitial fibrosis
Maintain surveillance with B-cell clonality studies to detect transformation to a lymphoproliferative disorder such as MALT lymphoma
Coordinate care across respiratory medicine, rheumatology and immunology
